name: Ink, Tea and Woodblocks: A Thousand Years of Japanese Arts
description: From a court lady's long story to Hokusai's wave, Kurosawa's samurai and Miyazaki's animation: Japan's literature, theatre, prints, film, tea and gardens over a thousand years.

checkpoints.name: Court and capital
checkpoints.note: Woodblock printing is used for Buddhist texts, the kimono takes shape and the imperial court makes an art of viewing cherry blossoms. Around 1010 the court lady Murasaki Shikibu writes The Tale of Genji, often called the first great novel.

checkpoints.name: Quiet arts
checkpoints.note: Noh, a masked drama of music and slow movement, is refined in the 1300s, the Golden Pavilion of Kinkaku-ji rises over its garden pond in 1397, and the tea ceremony takes shape in the 1500s as a discipline of calm and hospitality.

checkpoints.name: The Edo peace
checkpoints.note: The long peace of the shoguns brings the lively theatre of Kabuki, the poet Matsuo Basho and his haiku, and the colourful ukiyo-e prints of city life. Hokusai's Great Wave off Kanagawa appears around 1831, and Hiroshige's prints of travel and the seasons follow.

checkpoints.name: Pictures and novels
checkpoints.note: As Japan opens to the world its artists answer: anime begins in the 1910s, Yasunari Kawabata publishes his first stories in the 1920s, and after the war Osamu Tezuka begins the manga that will shape the form.

checkpoints.name: Screens and novels
checkpoints.note: Kurosawa's Rashomon and Seven Samurai, with Toshiro Mifune, Tokyo Story and Godzilla bring Japanese cinema abroad. Kawabata wins the Nobel Prize in 1968, Yayoi Kusama's dots fill galleries, Hayao Miyazaki's Studio Ghibli makes its animated films, and Haruki Murakami becomes one of the most translated novelists.
